title: Finance before Day One
summary: A starter guide to finance and accounting for MBA entrants with no finance background: eight short parts, a practice workbook, and a case to solve at the end.

chapters.title: Start here
chapters.markdown:
### How to use this guide

1. **Read one part at a time:** each part takes about 30 minutes. Parts 1 to 3 give the language, parts 4 to 7 give the tools, and part 8 is a case to solve.
2. **Keep the workbook open:** every part links to a tab in the [practice workbook](content/prep/files/finance-before-day-one-workbook.xlsx). Download it and open it in Excel or Google Sheets, then change the blue numbers and watch the rest move. This is how we learn what drives what.
3. **Do the check-yourself questions:** each part ends with two or three. Answers are at the end of the guide.
4. **Solve the case:** part 8 pulls everything together. Write your answer before you look at anyone else's.

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "A note on units", "icon": "fa-key", "text": "Indian businesses count in lakh and crore. 1 lakh = ₹1,00,000 and 1 crore = ₹1,00,00,000 = 100 lakh. In this guide, ₹ lakh is used for company figures, so Corner Cup's revenue of ₹180 lakh means ₹1.8 crore."}
```

### Meet Corner Cup

Corner Cup is a made-up café chain with three outlets in one city. It sells coffee, tea and bakery items to walk-in customers and through a delivery app. We follow it through one financial year, FY 2025-26 (1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026).

| Fact | FY 2025-26 |
|---|---:|
| Outlets | 3 |
| Revenue | ₹180 lakh |
| Average bill | ₹250 |
| Bills per outlet per day | About 67 |
| Net profit | ₹12 lakh |
| Bank loan at year end | ₹30 lakh |
| Cash at year end | ₹12 lakh |

chapters.title: The language of money
chapters.markdown:
**Finance** is the management of money: how a business raises it, spends it, invests it and returns it to the people who provided it. **Accounting** is the system that records all of this so that anyone can see what happened. In an MBA, we use accounting to read a business and finance to decide what it should do next.

### The five buckets

Every transaction, from a ₹250 cappuccino to a ₹25 lakh new outlet, lands in one of five buckets. Three of them describe what the business has on one date. Two of them describe what happened over a period.

![The five buckets: assets, liabilities, equity, income, expenses](content/prep/files/finance-before-day-one/d01_buckets.png)

1. **Assets:** what the business owns or is owed, that will bring value later. e.g. Corner Cup's espresso machines, the milk in the fridge, the cash in the bank, the money a delivery app has not yet paid.
2. **Liabilities:** what the business owes to outsiders. e.g. the bank loan, and the bill from the milk supplier that is due next month.
3. **Equity:** the owners' share, which is what is left for them after all liabilities are paid. It is the money they put in plus the profits they chose to keep in the business.
4. **Income (revenue):** what the business earns by selling. e.g. coffee and food sales.
5. **Expenses:** what the business uses up to earn that income. e.g. rent, staff salaries, milk and coffee beans. Hence profit is simply income minus expenses.

### Twenty words you will hear in week one

| Term | Plain meaning | Corner Cup example |
|---|---:|---:|
| Revenue (sales, turnover) | Value of what was sold in the period | ₹180 lakh of food and drinks |
| Cost of goods sold (COGS) | Cost of the items that were sold | Milk, beans, bakery items: ₹57.6 lakh |
| Gross profit | Revenue minus COGS | ₹122.4 lakh |
| Operating expenses (opex) | Day-to-day running costs | Rent, staff, power, marketing |
| EBITDA | Profit from operations before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation | ₹27.5 lakh |
| Net profit (PAT) | What is left after every cost and tax | ₹12 lakh |
| Fixed cost | Stays the same whether sales go up or down | Rent of ₹75,000 per outlet per month |
| Variable cost | Moves with every unit sold | ₹80 of ingredients in every ₹250 bill |
| Capital expenditure (capex) | Money spent on things that last years | New espresso machines |
| Depreciation | Spreading the cost of a long-life asset over its life | ₹8 lakh this year |
| Receivables (debtors) | Money customers owe us | Delivery app payouts due: ₹4.5 lakh |
| Payables (creditors) | Money we owe suppliers | Supplier bills due: ₹6 lakh |
| Inventory (stock) | Goods held to sell or use | ₹2.5 lakh of beans, milk and packaging |
| Working capital | Short-term assets minus short-term liabilities | Stock + receivables + cash − payables |
| Cash flow | Actual money moving in and out of the bank | ₹2 lakh more cash at year end |
| Budget | A plan of what we expect to earn and spend | Next year's sales target per outlet |
| Margin | A profit figure as a % of revenue | Net margin 6.7% |
| Leverage | Using borrowed money | Debt to equity 0.7x |
| Cost centre | A unit whose costs are tracked separately | Each outlet, or the central kitchen |
| Write-off | Removing an amount we will never recover | A corporate client who shut down and never paid |

### The Indian financial year

A **financial year (FY)** is the 12-month period a business uses to measure its results. In India it runs from 1 April to 31 March, so FY 2025-26 ends on 31 March 2026. Hence a café's busy Christmas season and the slower summer both fall in one financial year.

1. **Q1 (April to June):** books for the previous year are closed and audited. Listed companies hold their annual general meeting later in the year.
2. **Q2 (July to September):** listed companies announce Q1 results, and first-half reviews begin.
3. **Q3 (October to December):** mid-year review of the budget against actual sales.
4. **Q4 (January to March):** the Union Budget in February can change tax rates, and the next year's budget is prepared before 31 March.

Companies also pay advance tax in instalments during the year rather than all at once at the end.

### Check yourself

1. Corner Cup owes ₹6 lakh to its milk and coffee suppliers. Which of the five buckets is this?
2. Which bucket does the money the owners first put into the business belong to?
3. Write ₹1.8 crore in lakh.

chapters.title: The three financial statements
chapters.markdown:
A **financial statement** is a standard report that shows a business's results or position in a format everyone understands. There are three, and each answers one question.

1. **Profit and loss statement (P&L, income statement):** did we earn more than we spent during the period? It covers a period, such as a year.
2. **Balance sheet:** what do we own and owe on one date? It is a snapshot, such as on 31 March.
3. **Cash flow statement:** where did the cash come from and where did it go? It covers the same period as the P&L.

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "Key idea", "icon": "fa-key", "text": "The P&L is a film of the year. The balance sheet is a photo taken on the last day. The cash flow statement follows only the money in the bank."}
```

### Corner Cup's three statements, in short

Profit and loss, FY 2025-26 (₹ lakh). Full version in the **P&L tab**.

| Line | ₹ lakh |
|---|---:|
| Revenue | 180.0 |
| Less: all costs, interest and tax | −168.0 |
| **Net profit** | **12.0** |
| Less: dividend paid to owners | −2.0 |
| **Profit kept in the business** | **10.0** |

Balance sheet (₹ lakh). Full version in the **Balance sheet tab**.

|  | 31 Mar 2025 | 31 Mar 2026 |
|---|---:|---:|
| Net fixed assets (machines, fit-outs) | 58.0 | 60.0 |
| Inventory | 2.0 | 2.5 |
| Receivables | 3.0 | 4.5 |
| Cash | 10.0 | 12.0 |
| **Total assets** | **73.0** | **79.0** |
| Bank loan | 35.0 | 30.0 |
| Payables | 5.0 | 6.0 |
| Share capital | 20.0 | 20.0 |
| Retained earnings (profits kept) | 13.0 | 23.0 |
| **Total liabilities and equity** | **73.0** | **79.0** |

Cash flow, FY 2025-26 (₹ lakh). Full version in the **Cash flow tab**.

|  | ₹ lakh |
|---|---:|
| Cash from operating activities (running the cafés) | 19.0 |
| Cash from investing activities (new machines) | −10.0 |
| Cash from financing activities (loan repaid, dividend) | −7.0 |
| **Net change in cash** | **2.0** |

### How the statements connect

![How the P&L, cash flow and balance sheet connect](content/prep/files/finance-before-day-one/d04_link.png)

1. **Profit feeds equity:** the profit kept (₹10 lakh) is added to retained earnings on the balance sheet, which rise from ₹13 lakh to ₹23 lakh.
2. **Cash flow explains the cash line:** opening cash of ₹10 lakh plus the year's net cash flow of ₹2 lakh equals the ₹12 lakh of cash on the closing balance sheet.
3. **Non-cash costs are added back:** depreciation reduced profit but no money left the bank, so the cash flow statement adds it back.

### Accrual vs cash: revenue is not collection

**Accrual accounting** records income when it is earned and costs when they are incurred, whether or not money has moved. **Cash accounting** records them only when money moves. Companies in India must use accrual accounting, thus revenue and cash collected can differ.

e.g. Corner Cup delivers a ₹50,000 office catering order on 28 March 2026 and is paid on 10 April 2026. The ₹50,000 is revenue in FY 2025-26, because that is when it was earned, but the cash arrives in FY 2026-27. Until then it sits in receivables.

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "Try it in the workbook", "icon": "fa-table-cells", "text": "Open the **Balance sheet tab** and change closing receivables from 4.5 to 10. Watch closing cash fall in the Cash flow tab while net profit stays at ₹12 lakh."}
```

### Check yourself

1. Corner Cup made ₹12 lakh of net profit but its cash rose by only ₹2 lakh. Using the cash flow statement, where did the rest go?
2. The ₹50,000 catering order above: in which financial year is it revenue, and in which year is it cash?

chapters.title: How transactions are recorded
chapters.markdown:
In an MBA you will rarely record entries yourself, but you need to know how the numbers got into the statements, so that you can question them.

### The accounting equation

The **accounting equation** says that everything a business owns was paid for either by outsiders or by its owners: **Assets = Liabilities + Equity**. It holds after every single transaction.

![Corner Cup's accounting equation: 79 = 36 + 43](content/prep/files/finance-before-day-one/d02_equation.png)

### Double entry: every transaction has two sides

**Double entry** means every transaction is recorded in at least two accounts, once as a **debit** and once as a **credit**, for the same total. Debit and credit are not good and bad. They are simply the left and right sides of an account.

| Bucket | A debit (Dr) | A credit (Cr) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Assets | Increases it | Decreases it |
| Expenses | Increases it | Decreases it |
| Liabilities | Decreases it | Increases it |
| Equity | Decreases it | Increases it |
| Income | Decreases it | Increases it |

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "A way to remember it", "icon": "fa-key", "text": "DEAD CLIC: **D**ebits increase **E**xpenses, **A**ssets and **D**rawings (money owners take out). **C**redits increase **L**iabilities, **I**ncome and **C**apital (equity)."}
```

### Four Corner Cup entries

| Transaction | Debit | Credit |
|---|---:|---:|
| A customer pays ₹250 by UPI | Bank ₹250 (asset up) | Sales ₹250 (income up) |
| A delivery app order of ₹500, paid to us after 7 days | Receivable ₹500 (asset up) | Sales ₹500 (income up) |
| Seven days later the app pays | Bank ₹500 (asset up) | Receivable ₹500 (asset down) |
| Rent of ₹2,25,000 for the month is paid | Rent expense ₹2,25,000 | Bank ₹2,25,000 (asset down) |
| A ₹5 lakh espresso machine: ₹2 lakh paid now, ₹3 lakh by bank loan | Machinery ₹5,00,000 | Bank ₹2,00,000 and Loan ₹3,00,000 |

The last one is a **compound entry**: more than two accounts are involved, but the debits (₹5 lakh) still equal the credits (₹2 lakh + ₹3 lakh).

### From entry to statement

![Transaction to journal to ledger to trial balance to statements](content/prep/files/finance-before-day-one/d03_flow.png)

1. **Journal:** every transaction is first written down in date order, with its debit and credit. This is the diary of the business.
2. **Ledger:** entries are then sorted by account (cash, sales, rent, loan), so we can see the balance of each.
3. **Trial balance:** a list of every ledger balance, used to check that total debits equal total credits. It is a check, not a statement.
4. **Financial statements:** income and expense balances form the P&L, and asset, liability and equity balances form the balance sheet.

Today, software such as Tally or Zoho Books does steps 2 to 4 automatically once the entry is made. Hence the quality of the statements depends on entries being made correctly in step 1.

### Check yourself

1. Write the entry: Corner Cup buys ₹40,000 of coffee beans on 30 days' credit.
2. A trial balance shows total debits of ₹10,00,000 and total credits of ₹9,95,000. What does this tell us?

chapters.title: Costs and profit
chapters.markdown:
### Cost vs expense A **cost** is what we pay to acquire something. An **expense** is the part of that cost used up in earning this period's revenue. e.g. Corner Cup buys ₹58.1 lakh of ingredients in the year, but only the ₹57.6 lakh actually used in sales is an expense. The rest is still on the shelf as inventory, an asset. ### Cost of goods sold **Cost of goods sold (COGS)** is the cost of the items sold in the period. We find it from stock levels: ```msv-block {"type": "callout", "heading": "Formula", "icon": "fa-key", "text": "COGS = Opening stock + Purchases − Closing stock
Corner Cup: ₹2.0 lakh + ₹58.1 lakh − ₹2.5 lakh = ₹57.6 lakh, which is 32% of revenue."} ``` ### The revenue ladder The P&L is best read as a ladder. We start with revenue and take away one type of cost at each step. Each step has a name, and each name answers a different question. ![Waterfall from revenue 180 to retained 10](content/prep/files/finance-before-day-one/d05_ladder.png) 1. **Gross profit (₹122.4 lakh):** revenue minus COGS. Is the product itself profitable? A 68% gross margin is normal for a café, because a cup of coffee costs little to make. 2. **EBITDA (₹27.5 lakh):** gross profit minus operating expenses such as rent and staff. Are the cafés profitable to run? Investors compare businesses on this line because it ignores how they are financed and how old their assets are. 3. **EBIT (₹19.5 lakh):** EBITDA minus depreciation and amortisation. Also called operating profit. 4. **Profit before tax (₹16 lakh):** EBIT minus interest on borrowings. 5. **Net profit or PAT (₹12 lakh):** profit after tax. This belongs to the owners. 6. **Retained earnings (₹10 lakh):** net profit minus dividends. This is the profit kept to grow the business. ```msv-block {"type": "callout", "heading": "Try it in the workbook", "icon": "fa-table-cells", "text": "In the **P&L tab**, raise the food and drink cost from 32% to 36%. Gross profit falls by ₹7.2 lakh, and net profit falls from ₹12 lakh to ₹6.6 lakh. A four-point change in one cost line nearly halves the owners' profit."} ``` ### Capex vs opex **Capital expenditure (capex)** is money spent on assets that help the business for more than a year, such as machines or an outlet fit-out. **Operating expenditure (opex)** is the cost of running the business this year, such as rent or salaries. ![Capex goes to the balance sheet and reaches the P&L as depreciation; opex goes straight to the P&L](content/prep/files/finance-before-day-one/d06_capex.png) 1. **Where it goes:** capex is shown on the balance sheet as an asset. Opex goes straight to the P&L as an expense. 2. **When it hits profit:** capex reaches the P&L slowly, as depreciation spread over the asset's life. Opex reduces this year's profit in full. 3. **Why it matters:** spending ₹5 lakh on a machine does not cut this year's profit by ₹5 lakh, but it does cut this year's cash by ₹5 lakh. Thus profit and cash can move in very different ways. ### Depreciation **Depreciation** is the yearly charge that spreads the cost of an asset over the years it is used. It is a non-cash expense: the cash left when the asset was bought, not when it is depreciated. 1. **Straight line method (SLM):** the same amount every year. (Cost − value at the end) ÷ useful life. e.g. (₹5,00,000 − ₹50,000) ÷ 5 years = ₹90,000 a year. 2. **Written down value method (WDV):** a fixed percentage of the value still left each year, so the charge is higher in early years. e.g. at 25%, year 1 is ₹1,25,000, year 2 is ₹93,750, and so on. Indian income tax rules use this method. ![Book value of a 5 lakh machine under SLM and WDV](content/prep/files/finance-before-day-one/d07_depreciation.png) ```msv-block {"type": "callout", "heading": "Try it in the workbook", "icon": "fa-table-cells", "text": "The **Depreciation tab** has both schedules. Change the useful life to 8 years and see the yearly SLM charge fall."} ``` ### Fixed costs, variable costs and break-even A **fixed cost** stays the same whatever the sales, such as rent. A **variable cost** rises with each unit sold, such as the milk in each cup. The difference between the price and the variable cost is the **contribution**: what each sale leaves over to pay the fixed costs. 1. **Contribution per bill:** ₹250 average bill − ₹80 of ingredients = ₹170. 2. **Fixed costs per outlet per month:** about ₹2,63,600 (staff, rent, power, marketing and other costs, all treated as fixed here to keep it simple). 3. **Break-even bills:** fixed costs ÷ contribution = ₹2,63,600 ÷ ₹170 = about 1,551 bills a month, or 52 a day. 4. **Margin of safety:** each outlet serves about 2,000 bills a month, so sales can fall by 22% before the outlet makes a loss. ![Break-even chart for one Corner Cup outlet](content/prep/files/finance-before-day-one/d08_breakeven.png) ```msv-block {"type": "callout", "heading": "Try it in the workbook", "icon": "fa-table-cells", "text": "In the **Break-even tab**, raise the average bill from ₹250 to ₹275. Break-even falls from 52 to about 47 bills a day. Pricing is often the fastest lever a small business has."} ``` ### Check yourself 1. Opening stock is ₹1 lakh, purchases are ₹6 lakh and closing stock is ₹1.5 lakh. What is COGS? 2. Is a ₹3 lakh renovation of seating that will last five years capex or opex? How does it reach the P&L? 3. If rent rises by ₹30,000 a month for each outlet, what is the new break-even in bills a month?

chapters.title: Cash and working capital
chapters.markdown:
**Working capital** is the money tied up in running the business day to day: stock on the shelves and money owed by customers, minus money we owe to suppliers. A profitable business can still fail if too much cash is stuck here.

### Three numbers that decide cash

1. **Inventory days:** how long stock sits before it is sold. Inventory ÷ COGS × 365. Corner Cup: 2.5 ÷ 57.6 × 365 = 16 days.
2. **Receivable days:** how long customers take to pay. Receivables ÷ revenue × 365. Corner Cup: 4.5 ÷ 180 × 365 = 9 days, mostly delivery app payouts.
3. **Payable days:** how long we take to pay suppliers. Payables ÷ COGS × 365. Corner Cup: 6 ÷ 57.6 × 365 = 38 days.

The **cash conversion cycle (CCC)** joins them: inventory days + receivable days − payable days. It is the number of days our own cash is stuck before it comes back.

![Corner Cup's cash conversion cycle of minus 13 days](content/prep/files/finance-before-day-one/d09_ccc.png)

Corner Cup's cycle is negative (−13 days): customers pay at the counter, while suppliers wait 38 days. Thus suppliers are funding part of the business. This is why cafés, supermarkets and quick-service restaurants can grow quickly on little cash. e.g. D-Mart is known for paying suppliers quickly in return for better prices, which shows that a business can also choose to give up this benefit on purpose.

A business that sells to other businesses on credit is the opposite. It pays for flour and wages first and waits months to be paid, so the faster it grows, the more cash it needs. The case in Part 8 is about exactly this.

### Profit is not cash

![Opening cash 10 plus operating 19 minus investing 10 minus financing 7 equals closing 12](content/prep/files/finance-before-day-one/d10_cashbridge.png)

1. **Timing:** revenue is counted when earned, cash when received. Rising receivables mean profit is ahead of cash.
2. **Capex:** a new machine takes cash today but reaches profit slowly through depreciation.
3. **Financing:** repaying a loan or paying a dividend uses cash but is not an expense, so it never appears in profit.

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "Try it in the workbook", "icon": "fa-table-cells", "text": "The **Working capital tab** calculates all three days. Change closing receivables on the Balance sheet tab and watch both the cycle and the cash move."}
```

### Check yourself

1. Corner Cup's receivables are ₹4.5 lakh, about 9 days of sales. If they equalled 30 days of sales, how much would receivables be, and how much more cash would be tied up?
2. Why can a café run with a negative cash conversion cycle when a bakery that supplies offices on credit usually cannot?

chapters.title: Reading statements like an analyst
chapters.markdown:
A **ratio** compares two numbers from the statements so that we can judge a business regardless of its size. A ratio on its own says little. We compare it with the same business last year, and with similar businesses.

![Four families of ratios with Corner Cup values](content/prep/files/finance-before-day-one/d11_ratios.png)

| Ratio | Formula | Corner Cup | What it tells us |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Gross margin | Gross profit ÷ revenue | 68.0% | How much of each sale is left after the product cost |
| Net margin | Net profit ÷ revenue | 6.7% | What the owners keep from each ₹100 of sales |
| Return on equity (ROE) | Net profit ÷ average equity | 31.6% | The return on the owners' money |
| Return on capital employed (ROCE) | EBIT ÷ (debt + equity) | 26.7% | The return on all long-term money in the business |
| Current ratio | Current assets ÷ current liabilities | 3.2x | Whether short-term bills are covered |
| Debt to equity | Borrowings ÷ equity | 0.7x | How much of the business is funded by lenders |
| Interest cover | EBIT ÷ interest | 5.6x | How many times profit covers the interest bill |
| Asset turnover | Revenue ÷ total assets | 2.3x | Sales generated for each ₹1 of assets |

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "Try it in the workbook", "icon": "fa-table-cells", "text": "Every ratio in the **Ratios tab** links back to the statements. Change any input on the P&L tab and see which ratios move and which do not."}
```

### How to read a real annual report

Every listed Indian company publishes an annual report, which we can download from its investor relations page or from the BSE and NSE websites.

1. **Step 1, the story:** read the Management Discussion and Analysis section. Here the management explains what happened and why.
2. **Step 2, the right statements:** go to the consolidated statements, which include all subsidiaries, rather than the standalone ones.
3. **Step 3, the three statements:** read the P&L, balance sheet and cash flow, with this year and last year side by side.
4. **Step 4, the notes:** for any large or surprising number, read its note, such as the split of revenue or the list of borrowings.
5. **Step 5, the ratios:** work out five or six ratios and compare them with a competitor. e.g. compare Jubilant FoodWorks (which runs Domino's in India) with Westlife Foodworld (which runs McDonald's in west and south India).

### Check yourself

1. If Corner Cup used ₹8 lakh of its cash to buy a new machine, what would its current ratio become?
2. Two cafés both have a 7% net margin. One has debt to equity of 0.7x, the other 3x. Which is riskier, and why?

chapters.title: Money over time
chapters.markdown:
The **time value of money** means that ₹1 today is worth more than ₹1 received later, because money we have today can be invested to earn a return. Hence we cannot add up rupees from different years as if they were the same.

![Compounding and discounting on a timeline](content/prep/files/finance-before-day-one/d12_tvm.png)

1. **Future value (compounding):** what an amount today will grow to. Amount × (1 + rate)<sup>years</sup>. e.g. ₹1,00,000 at 8% for 5 years = ₹1,46,933.
2. **Present value (discounting):** what a future amount is worth today. Amount ÷ (1 + rate)<sup>years</sup>. e.g. ₹1,00,000 due in 5 years at 8% is worth ₹68,058 today.
3. **Discount rate:** the return we could earn elsewhere at similar risk. The riskier the project, the higher the rate we use.

### Net present value: should Corner Cup open a fourth outlet?

**Net present value (NPV)** is the present value of all the cash a project brings in, minus what it costs today. If NPV is above zero, the project earns more than the discount rate, so we should go ahead.

The fourth outlet costs ₹25 lakh to open and is expected to bring in ₹7 lakh of cash a year for 6 years. Corner Cup's owners want at least 12% a year.

![Present value of each year's cash for the fourth outlet](content/prep/files/finance-before-day-one/d13_npv.png)

1. **Add up the cash as received:** 6 × ₹7 lakh = ₹42 lakh. This looks like a large gain, but it ignores time.
2. **Discount each year to today:** the six present values add up to ₹28.78 lakh.
3. **Subtract the cost:** ₹28.78 lakh − ₹25 lakh = **NPV of +₹3.78 lakh**. The outlet earns more than 12%, so it is worth opening.
4. **Internal rate of return (IRR):** the discount rate at which NPV is exactly zero. Here it is 17.2%, which is above the 12% the owners want.
5. **Payback:** ₹25 lakh ÷ ₹7 lakh = 3.6 years. Payback is simple to explain but ignores time value and everything after the payback year, so use it only as a rough check.

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "Try it in the workbook", "icon": "fa-table-cells", "text": "In the **Time value tab**, change the yearly cash from 7 to 6. NPV turns negative. Then change the discount rate to see how sensitive the decision is."}
```

### Check yourself

1. What is the present value of ₹50,000 received in 3 years, at 10% a year?
2. If the fourth outlet brought in ₹6 lakh a year instead of ₹7 lakh, would you open it at a 12% discount rate?

chapters.title: Case study: Sunrise Bakehouse: profitable, but short of cash
chapters.markdown:
```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "Your task", "icon": "fa-pen-to-square", "text": "Read the case, then solve it in the **Case - Sunrise tab** of the workbook (download it first). Fill in the yellow cells, then write a recommendation of no more than five lines, as if you were advising the owner. Allow about 90 minutes."}
```

### The situation

Sunrise Bakehouse is a made-up bakery owned by Anita. For years it has sold bread, cakes and puffs through its own shop. In FY 2025-26 it won contracts to supply the canteens of several large offices nearby. Revenue rose by half and profit rose by 69%. Anita bought a new oven line to keep up.

In March 2026 the bank calls her. Her overdraft, which was zero a year ago, is now ₹12 lakh out of a ₹20 lakh limit. Cash in the bank has fallen from ₹15 lakh to ₹3.5 lakh. Anita is confused: "We have never made more money. How can we be short of cash?"

![Sunrise Bakehouse: profit up, cash down](content/prep/files/finance-before-day-one/d14_sunrise.png)

At the same time, a large office park has offered her a new contract worth ₹40 lakh of sales a year, on the same terms as the others. Anita wants to sign it next week.

### The numbers (₹ lakh)

| Profit and loss | FY 2024-25 | FY 2025-26 |
|---|---:|---:|
| Revenue: walk-in shop | 80.0 | 80.0 |
| Revenue: office canteen contracts | 40.0 | 100.0 |
| **Total revenue** | **120.0** | **180.0** |
| Cost of goods sold | 54.0 | 81.0 |
| Operating expenses | 48.0 | 70.0 |
| Depreciation | 4.0 | 5.0 |
| Interest | 1.0 | 2.0 |
| Tax (25%) | 3.25 | 5.5 |
| **Net profit** | **9.75** | **16.5** |

| Balance sheet, 31 March | 2025 | 2026 |
|---|---:|---:|
| Net fixed assets | 30.0 | 45.0 |
| Inventory | 6.0 | 12.0 |
| Receivables | 10.0 | 30.0 |
| Cash | 15.0 | 3.5 |
| **Total assets** | **61.0** | **90.5** |
| Payables | 8.0 | 9.0 |
| Bank overdraft (limit ₹20 lakh, 12% a year) | 0.0 | 12.0 |
| Long-term loan | 10.0 | 10.0 |
| Share capital | 20.0 | 20.0 |
| Retained earnings (no dividend paid) | 23.0 | 39.5 |
| **Total liabilities and equity** | **61.0** | **90.5** |

### Other facts

- Capex in FY 2025-26 was ₹20 lakh, for the new oven line.
- The office contracts say customers will pay within 90 days. In practice they pay in about 110 days.
- Anita could offer the offices a 2% discount if they pay within 15 days.
- The new ₹40 lakh contract would be on the same terms as the current office contracts.

### Questions

1. **Profitability:** work out the gross margin and net margin for both years. Has the business become less profitable?
2. **Working capital:** work out receivable days, inventory days, payable days and the cash conversion cycle for both years. What changed most?
3. **Cash flow:** build the FY 2025-26 cash flow statement from the numbers above (operating, investing, financing). Check that it explains the fall in cash from ₹15 lakh to ₹3.5 lakh.
4. **Cost of the discount:** what yearly interest rate does the 2% early payment discount equal? Hint: discount ÷ (1 − discount) × 365 ÷ days saved. Is it cheaper or dearer than the overdraft?
5. **If every office takes the discount:** how much cash would be released, how much discount would Anita give away in a year, and how much interest would she save?
6. **The new contract:** on today's terms, how much extra would be tied up in receivables? Could the overdraft fund it?
7. **Recommendation:** in no more than five lines, tell Anita what to do and why. Use your numbers.

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "How to present your answer", "icon": "fa-table-cells", "text": "Use the order an MBA case discussion expects: **situation** (one line), **problem** (what is really wrong), **numbers** (the three or four that prove it), **options** (two or three, each with its cost), and **recommendation** (what to do first, and what to track every month)."}
```

chapters.title: Answers to the check-yourself questions
chapters.markdown:
### Part 1

1. A liability (payables, or sundry creditors).
2. Equity (share capital).
3. ₹180 lakh.

### Part 2

1. Profit of ₹12 lakh plus depreciation of ₹8 lakh, less ₹1 lakh more tied up in working capital, gave ₹19 lakh from operations. ₹10 lakh went on new machines, ₹5 lakh on repaying the loan and ₹2 lakh on the dividend, leaving ₹2 lakh.
2. Revenue in FY 2025-26, because it was earned on 28 March 2026. Cash in FY 2026-27, when it arrives on 10 April.

### Part 3

1. Debit Inventory (or Purchases) ₹40,000. Credit Payables (the supplier) ₹40,000. No cash moves yet.
2. There is an error: an entry was posted on one side only, or with the wrong amount, or to the wrong side. It must be found and fixed before the statements are prepared.

### Part 4

1. ₹1 lakh + ₹6 lakh − ₹1.5 lakh = ₹5.5 lakh.
2. Capex, because it benefits the business for five years. It goes on the balance sheet and reaches the P&L as depreciation, e.g. ₹60,000 a year under the straight line method with no value at the end.
3. Fixed costs rise to about ₹2,93,600 a month. ₹2,93,600 ÷ ₹170 = about 1,727 bills a month, or 58 a day.

### Part 5

1. ₹180 lakh × 30 ÷ 365 = about ₹14.8 lakh of receivables, so about ₹10.3 lakh more cash would be tied up.
2. A café is paid at the counter but pays its suppliers about a month later. A bakery supplying offices pays for flour and wages first and then waits months to be paid, so its cash is out much longer.

### Part 6

1. Current assets fall from ₹19 lakh to ₹11 lakh. ₹11 lakh ÷ ₹6 lakh = 1.8x.
2. The café with debt to equity of 3x. Its interest and loan repayments are due whatever its sales, so a bad year could leave it unable to pay the bank.

### Part 7

1. ₹50,000 ÷ 1.10<sup>3</sup> = ₹50,000 ÷ 1.331 = ₹37,566.
2. No. Six years of ₹6 lakh are worth ₹24.67 lakh today at 12%, which is less than the ₹25 lakh cost, so NPV is about −₹0.33 lakh. It is close, so a small change in the forecast would change the answer.

*All businesses, people and figures in this guide are made up for teaching. Real company and software names appear only as public examples.*
